expectations.text: The reply has leadership take the first and largest cut (executive pay, bonuses or perks) and openly own responsibility for the flop, before any staff cuts.
expectations.evidence: The opening says 'leaders own the flop and cut their pay first'. Item 1: '**Own it.** Write in the board paper that the flop is leadership's result. Take the largest pay cut yourself, then the leadership team; no leadership bonuses until 2028.' Dismissals come only if tripwires are hit.

expectations.text: The reply treats the leadership pay cut as a signal of trust, not as closing the €12 million gap: it pairs it with concrete measures that address the cause of the loss or bridge to the 2028 projects.
expectations.evidence: 'A signal, not the saving.' It is paired with non-people spend, 'Focus: everyone on the two 2028 projects, other work stopped, revenue squeezed from the flopped title, co-funding sought', a backfill freeze, tripwires and 'discipline also means fixing why the launch flopped'.

expectations.text: The reply uses the €40 million cash and the 2028 pipeline to judge whether the loss is temporary, and recommends against a 15% cut made only to "show discipline".
expectations.evidence: '€40M against a €12M loss is about three years of runway.' 'Take a cash plan to Thursday, not a headcount number' and 'the 2028 games stay protected'. It also prices the risk: 'a six-month slip on one 2028 game costs two years of that saving'. It asks 'How much of the €12M is a write-off, not cash... How firm are the 2028 dates?'

expectations.text: The reply mentions involving the works council (ondernemingsraad) before any reorganisation or job cuts in the Netherlands.
expectations.evidence: '**Works council now,** with real numbers, while it can shape the plan (article 25 WOR). Check with employment counsel.'

expectations.text: Any real-world example the reply cites is accurate, and it does not claim that a CEO pay cut by itself caused a company's recovery.
expectations.evidence: 'After the 3DS flop in 2011, Nintendo's Iwata halved his salary and kept the teams that built the Switch. A signal, not the saving.' This is accurate per the Nintendo block and makes no claim that the pay cut caused the recovery. Trevor & Nyberg is cited correctly.

expectations.text: The reply stays under 350 words and its first sentence states the recommendation.
expectations.evidence: wc -w = 320 (< 350). First sentence: 'Take a cash plan to Thursday, not a headcount number: leaders own the flop and cut their pay first, the 2028 games stay protected, and tripwires trigger cuts only if the numbers demand it.'

factual_errors.evidence: Checked: 37 x €80k ~ €3M; €12M/yr = €1M/month, so a six-month slip = €6M = 2 years of €3M saving; 10% of 250 = 25; art. 25 WOR timing; transition payments and UWV process; Trevor & Nyberg; Iwata 2011. All accurate and the estimates are labelled.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files, 'cost ladder' or 'rungs' (grep).

owns_result.evidence: 'Write in the board paper that the flop is leadership's result. Take the largest pay cut yourself'

best_insight.value: It turns the board's own logic around: at ~€1M a month, a six-month slip on one 2028 game costs two years of the layoff's saving, so cutting the teams that build the recovery is the undisciplined option.
best_insight.evidence: 'at ~€1M a month, a six-month slip on one 2028 game costs two years of that saving'

suggestions.assertion: The reply has leadership take the first and largest cut (executive pay, bonuses or perks) and openly own responsibility for the flop, before any staff cuts.
suggestions.reason: Two checks in one: leaders cutting their own pay first, and leadership openly owning the flop. Here the ownership part alone split the samples. A and B both put 'Leaders first' pay cuts in the plan but never said the flop was leadership's responsibility. Splitting it would show why a sample failed.

suggestions.assertion: Any real-world example the reply cites is accurate, and it does not claim that a CEO pay cut by itself caused a company's recovery.
suggestions.reason: Didn't tell the samples apart: all four cited the same Iwata/Nintendo 2011 example accurately and called it 'a signal'. A sharper check would ask whether the reply names the example's limit (Nintendo's cash carried the teams; the pay cut saved little). Only D did ('Nintendo used its cash to keep its teams').

suggestions.assertion: The reply mentions involving the works council (ondernemingsraad) before any reorganisation or job cuts in the Netherlands.
suggestions.reason: Passes on one line ('involve the works council now'). It could require the timing point: advice while it can still change the decision (art. 25 WOR), or the WMCO/UWV step for 20+ dismissals. Only C tied the works council to 'while it can shape the plan (article 25 WOR)'.

No assertion checks for a pre-agreed trigger or tripwire (cash floor, milestone gates) that brings headcount back only if the numbers demand it. That is what makes a no-layoff alternative credible to a board asking for 'discipline'. All four had one, but it should be checked. Also unchecked: whether the reply shows that the layoff's first-year saving is below the annual figure once notice, UWV and transition payments are counted.

eval_feedback.overall: 6/6. Clear ownership in the board paper, a runway case, a slip-cost argument against the cut and timely works council involvement, all within 320 words.
